When this army had come together, they rode through the forest called Myrkviðr, which divides Húnaland and Gotaland. And when they came out of the forest, there were large settlements and level plains, and on the plains stood a fair fortress, and Hervör, sister of King Angantýr, ruled there, with Ormarr, her foster-father. They had been set there to guard the land against the army of the Huns, and they had a great force there. One morning at sunrise Hervör stood up on a tower above the fortress gate. She saw great clouds of dust from horses south towards the forest, so that they hid the sun for a long time. Next she saw a gleam beneath the dust-cloud, as if one looked on gold: fair shields overlaid with gold, gilded helmets and white mail-coats. She then saw that this was the army of the Huns, and a great multitude. Hervör went down quickly and calls a trumpeter and bade him sound the assembly of the troops. And then Hervör said: "Take your weapons and make ready for battle, and you, Ormarr, ride against the Huns and offer them battle before the southern gate of the fortress." Ormarr said:

Then he sent men out in all directions and summoned to him every man who was willing to give him support and could wield weapons. He then went to Dúnheiðr with his force, and that was a very great army. Then the army of the Huns came against him, and they had twice as many men. On the next day they began their battle and fought all that day, and in the evening they went to their camps. They fought thus for eight days, so that the chieftains were still unhurt, but no one knew the count of how many fell. But both day and night men streamed to Angantýr from all directions, and so it came about that he had no fewer people than at first. Now the battle grew still fiercer. The Huns were very fierce and saw their situation: that the only hope of life was if they won, and that it would go ill for them to ask the Goths for quarter. The Goths defended their freedom and their native land against the Huns, and so stood fast, and each urged on the other. As the day wore on, the Goths made so hard an attack that the ranks of the Huns bent before it. And when Angantýr saw that, he went forward out of the shield-wall and into the front of the battle-line, with Tyrfingr in his hand, and hewed both men and horses. Then the shield-wall broke before the kings of the Huns, and the brothers exchanged blows. There fell Hlöðr and King Humli, and then the Huns broke into flight, and the Goths slew them. .... c567cb029a80e6f7b2efff6eadcd38e4ddd27150.s: Skjöldr was the name of a son of Óðinn, from whom the Skjöldungar are descended. He had his seat and ruled the lands that are now called Danmörk, but were then called Gotland. Skjöldr had a son called Friðleifr, who ruled the lands after him. Friðleifr's son was called Fróði. He took the kingship after his father at the time when Augustus the emperor established peace over the whole world. At that time Christ was born. And because Fróði was the most powerful of all kings in the Northern lands, the peace was named after him throughout all the Danish-speaking lands, and the Norwegians call it Fróði's Peace. No man harmed another, even if he came upon his father's slayer or his brother's slayer, free or bound. There was then also no thief or robber, so that a gold ring lay for a long time on Jalangrsheiðr. King Fróði went on a visit to Svíþjóð [Sweden] to the king who is named Fjölnir. There he bought two slave-women, who were called Fenja and Menja. They were big and strong. At that time two millstones were found in Danmörk so large that no one was strong enough to turn them. And this property went with the mill, that whatever the one grinding asked for was ground out on the mill. That mill was called Grótti. The man who gave King Fróði the mill is named Hengikjöptr. King Fróði had the slave-women led to the mill and bade them grind gold and peace and happiness for Fróði. Then he gave them no longer rest or sleep than while the cuckoo was silent or a song could be spoken. It is said that they then spoke the poem that is called Gróttasöngr. And before the poem was ended, they ground an army against Fróði, so that in that night there came the sea-king who was called Mýsingr, and he killed Fróði and took great plunder there. Then Fróði's Peace came to an end. Mýsingr took Grótti with him, and Fenja and Menja too, and bade them grind salt. He bade them grind longer. They ground for a little while before the ships sank down, and there was afterwards a whirlpool in the sea, where the sea falls into the mill's eye. Then the sea became salt.

f50ce2310d99fb1a983f75946bd239fdd14b3030.s: There was a powerful man named Gestumblindi in Reiðgotaland. He was out of favour with King Heiðrekr. In the king's retinue there were seven men who were to judge all the cases of men in that land. King Heiðrekr sacrificed to Freyr. The largest boar he could get he was to give to Freyr. They held it so holy that over its bristles oaths were to be sworn in all great matters, and that boar was to be sacrificed at the atonement-sacrifice [sónarblót]. On Yule eve the atonement-boar was to be led into the hall before the king, and men then laid their hands on its bristles and made solemn vows. King Heiðrekr made the vow that no man should have done so much against him, if he came into his power, that he should not have the choice of receiving the judgement of his wise men. That man should also be inviolate before him if he put forward riddles which the king could not solve. But when men tried putting riddles to him, none was put forward that he did not solve. The king sent word to Gestumblindi that he should come to him, and set him a day; otherwise, the king said, he would have men come to him. Neither choice seemed good to him, because he knew himself ill-equipped to exchange words with the king. Nor did his prospects seem good if he had to take the judgement of the wise men, for the charges were many. He knows too that if the king's men come to him, it will cost him his life. Then he sacrificed to Óðinn and asked him for help and promised him great gifts. One evening a guest came to Gestumblindi. He called himself Gestumblindi. They were so alike that neither could be told from the other. They exchanged clothes, and the farmer went to hide himself, and everyone thought the farmer was there where the guest was. This man goes to meet the king and greets him. The king looked at him and was silent. Gestumblindi said: "I have come here, lord, because I want to be reconciled with you." The king asked: "Will you have the judgement of the wise men?" Gestumblindi said: "Are there no other ways out?" The king says: "You may put forward riddles. You shall be free if I do not see through them." Gestumblindi answers: "I am little fit for that, but the other course is hard." The king said: "Would you rather have the judgement?" "No," he says, "I would rather put forward the riddles." The king said: "That is also right, but much is at stake. If you defeat me, you shall have my daughter, and you shall not be refused that. But you seem unlikely to have great wisdom, and it has never yet happened that I did not see through the riddles that were put to me." Then a chair was set beneath Gestumblindi, and people looked forward to hearing wise words there. Then Gestumblindi said:

And now Óðinn had become angry with him, because he had struck at him, and that same night the king was killed.
